title: Oncall Observability Triage Checklist and Signal Catalog
summary: Practical checklist and signal catalog for SREs and engineers responding to inference anomalies. Emphasis on fast narrowing, reliable queries, and minimal dashboards that guide action.
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a compact, action-oriented triage checklist and signal catalog for on-call engineers. It is meant to be copied into runbook pages, used as the quick appendix for incident commanders, and be the canonical source for a minimal set of dashboard panels and alert suggestions focused on tokenized LLM inference workloads.

Audience:
On-call SREs, serving-runtime engineers, platform owners, and solutions engineers supporting customers during incidents.

Scope:
- Covers hosted and dedicated clusters, routing layer, and runtime batching/KV cache interactions.
- Excludes per-customer private deployment playbooks; those live in customer-specific docs.

Quick triage (0-10 minutes):
1) Confirm the alert: open the alert details and note labels (region, model, route, pool).
2) Determine blast radius: use redwood.request.count grouped by (region, model_version, route) to see where traffic is coming from.
3) Classify symptoms: errors vs latency vs cost vs throughput drop. Map to next steps: errors -> check logs/traces; latency -> traces + queue/batch metrics; cost -> token rates and fallback counts.
4) Announce: post one-line summary to #oncall-inference: what, where, initial hypothesis, mitigation in progress.

Essential signal catalog (canonical metric names we expect dashboards/alerts to use):
- redwood.request.count (counter) - total requests per route
- redwood.request.errors (counter; label status_code) - error counts split by 4xx/5xx
- redwood.latency_ms.p50/p90/p95/p99 (gauge/histogram_summary) - end-to-end server-side latency in ms
- redwood.tokens.out.rate (gauge) - emitted tokens per second per model
- redwood.batch.size.p50/p90 (gauge) - observed effective batch size in runtime
- redwood.batch.wait.ms (gauge) - time waiting to form a batch
- redwood.kv.hit_rate (gauge 0..1) - KV cache hit fraction by model_version
- redwood.kv.latency_ms.p95 (gauge) - KV lookup latency tail
- redwood.queue.depth (gauge) - pending requests in the batching queue per pool/host
- redwood.gpu.util.percent (gauge) - per-GPU utilization percent
- redwood.model.fallback.count (counter) - times router fell back to alternate variant
- redwood.stream.flush.count (counter) - partial streaming flushes detected

Suggested alert rules (starter, tune per-model):
- Elevated error rate (P1 if sustained): (increase of redwood.request.errors / redwood.request.count > 5% over 5m) AND affects >5% total traffic for 10m.
- Latency tail regression (P1): p95 > 1500ms AND p95 >= 2x baseline for 5m.
- Queue pressure (P2): redwood.queue.depth > 500 for pool or > 100 per host for 3m.
- KV cache regression (P2): drop in redwood.kv.hit_rate > 20% vs 24h median.
- Unexpected fallback storm (P2): redwood.model.fallback.count > 30 in 10m.

Minimal dashboard layout (panels that must be visible on first load):
Top / Overview row:
- Requests vs errors (timeseries) filtered by selected region/model. Query: sum(rate(redwood_request_count[1m])) by (region) and sum(rate(redwood_request_errors[1m])) by (region).
- Traffic heatmap by model_version (table) showing request rate and error_rate sparkline.
Performance row:
- Latency p50/p95/p99 per model (stacked lines with selectable model). Use histogram_quantile where available.
- Batch formation: batch.wait.ms and batch.size.p90 lines; annotate deploy events.
Infrastructure row:
- GPU utilization (per-instance bars) + counts of nodes above 90% util.
- Queue depth + host-level CPU IO wait as small multiples.
Diagnostics row:
- KV cache hit rate per model and kv.latency p95.
- Recent trace links (last 50 traces ordered by duration) with trace_id clickable to tracing UI.

Trace checklist (what spans/tags to inspect in representative traces):
Required spans we expect in trace payloads: request.ingress, request.tokenize, routing.choose, runtime.batch.wait, runtime.forward, kvcache.lookup, streaming.flush, request.respond.
Inspect tags on spans: model_version, batch_size, seq_len, gpu_id, host, pool, region, fallback_reason.
Common trace signals and quick interpretations:
- runtime.batch.wait long + batch_size small -> batching misconfiguration or sudden traffic shape change.
- runtime.forward long AND low GPU util -> model kernel mismatch or inefficient kernel path.
- kvcache.lookup p95 spiking and hit_rate low -> backend cache issue or eviction storm after reload.
- routing.choose shows many fallbacks -> upstream capacity/pool rebalancer problem.

Step-by-step triage playbook (detailed):
1) Scope: use request.count and error labels to narrow to region/model/pool.
2) Reproduce: if safe, run a small synthetic request against suspected model variant to capture a fresh trace.
3) Trace triage: pick 3 slow/failing traces across different hosts; compare runtime.forward durations and batch.wait distributions.
4) Infra check: inspect GPU util, host CPU IO wait, and network dev error counters for correlated spikes.
5) Routing check: inspect router metrics and routing.decide logs for increased fallback counts or weight shifts.
6) Mitigation options (choose least impactful first):
   - Route traffic away from failing model_version to last-good variant (canary rollback).
   - Scale pool capacity or enable burst capacity for Dedicated pools.
   - Temporarily tighten or apply rate limits for low-priority customers to reduce load.
   - If KV backend is unhealthy, disable local caching or reduce cache pressure while root cause is investigated.
7) Monitor: after mitigation, watch error rate and tail latency for 2x expected recovery window (10-30 minutes depending on mitigation).
8) Collect artifacts: metric snapshots (5m/1h/24h), 5 representative traces, deploy IDs, traffic-weight changes, and a short timeline. Attach to Jira ticket for postmortem.

Common hypotheses with simple validation steps (one-liners):
- New model kernel slower: validate by comparing runtime.forward durations between new and old variant using traces; if true, rollback or try alternative kernel flags.
- Cache eviction after reload: validate by checking kv.size_bytes and hit_rate around reload times; correlate with model load logs.
- Traffic pattern change causing poor batching: validate by looking at batch.size.p90 and batch.wait.ms; run a synthetic burst to measure formation.
- Network egress spike in AZ: validate by correlating region-level p95 with host network errors and net_dev counters.
- Slow client consumer for streaming: validate by streaming.flush.count and per-connection RTT; consider client-side guidance or smaller chunking.

Post-incident actions (short list for the ticket):
- Update dashboard annotations with incident summary and mitigation steps.
- If root cause points to missing metric, add instrumentation request with priority and owner.
- Review alert thresholds that caused noisy alerts; adjust or add suppressions.
- Schedule a short retro with platform/product if customer impact is significant.

Known instrumentation gaps (current backlog references):
- Per-GPU kernel selection counters and kernel.duration (INF-5022).
- request.stream.consumer_rtt metric for streaming slow-consumer detection.
- Per-model cold-start time series for Dedicated pool autoscaler tuning.

Appendix: PromQL examples (copy into dashboard panels):
- Error rate by region: sum(rate(redwood_request_errors[5m])) by (region) / sum(rate(redwood_request_count[5m])) by (region)
- p95 latency for a model: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_latency_bucket{model_version=~"my-model.*"}[5m])) by (le, model_version))
- Batch p90: quantile_over_time(0.9, redwood_batch_size_p{model_version!=""}[5m:1m])

Notes
- Keep dashboards small and action-oriented; prefer a short set of panels with trace links rather than a monolithic dashboard.
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic; for full taxonomy and naming conventions refer to the signal taxonomy doc in the observability space.
